NightJar is not active. Open Vector or LSPosed. Turn on the NightJar module with scope Phone Services. Then reboot the phone.
NightJar does not support this build yet. The module stopped itself in the phone service. Share diagnostics to help add support.
The module is newer than the app. Update NightJar to see all details.
No hidden messages yet. Most phones receive a few each day from voicemail and the carrier. Run a self-test to check detection.
The self-test checks detection inside Android. It cannot test messages that the modem handles alone.
Not seen yet. This type may not have arrived. The modem of your phone may handle it without telling Android.

Your messaging app showed this message. NightJar only counts these messages. NightJar does not record them.

The network sent a Type 0 message (protocol identifier 0x40), and the phone did not show it. A sender can use it to check that a phone is on, and it may show where the phone is. NightJar does not change the confirmation that the phone sends to the network.
The coding scheme of this message is class 0, so the phone shows it on the screen one time. Android normally does not save it.
The protocol identifier of this message is a replace type. The phone replaces an earlier message of the same type from the same sender. A sender can use it to change a message after you read it.
This message sets a waiting indicator, for example the voicemail icon. The coding scheme or the message header carries the indicator.
This message controls your visual voicemail app. Android gave it to that app and did not show it.
This message is a notice about a call that you missed. Android made a missed-call entry from it and did not show a message.
This message is for the carrier app on your phone ({package}). Android gave it to that app and did not show it.
This message configures chat features (RCS) for your number.
This message is only for {app}. Apps usually use these messages for sign-in codes. Your messaging app does not show it.
This message has data for port {port}, and Android does not show it. NightJar does not know an app that uses this port. Some apps use data messages, and attackers may use them to track phones.
This push message tells your messaging app about a picture message (MMS). It can be a new message, a delivery report or a read report. Your messaging app downloads the MMS itself.
This push message has a web link (Service Indication). Android does not show these messages by default.
This push message tries to change your network settings (APN or proxy). A PIN protects it, but carriers rarely send these messages today. An unexpected one can send your data through another server.
This push message asks the phone to contact a device management server, often the server of your carrier. The server can change settings or install updates.
This push message is a location request (SUPL). A location server asks the phone for its position, and the phone shows a notice. This is normal during emergency calls.
NightJar cannot read this push message, because its header is wrong: {anomaly}. Attackers can use damaged push messages to crash a phone. By default, NightJar blocks this type of message.
This push message has content type {contentType}. NightJar does not know this content type. Android gives it to the app that registered for that type, if one exists.
The protocol identifier of this message is 0x7F, so the phone gives it to the SIM. Carriers use these messages to update the SIM. If you block it, the SIM may not get updates from the carrier.
The coding scheme of this message is class 2, so the phone saved it on the SIM. Your messaging app may not show it.
This is a delivery report for a message that this phone sent. It tells the phone if the message arrived.
Software from the phone maker handled this message ({detail}).
This message did not come from the network. An app ({package}) added it to the SMS system of the phone. An app can use this to make a false message look real.
{app} sent a message to {number} without your messaging app. Android saved the message in your messages.
{app} sent a message to {number} without your messaging app. Android did not save the message in your messages.
{app} sent a data message to {number}, port {port}. Data messages never appear in your messaging app.
{app} sent a raw SMS packet to {number}. It did not use the normal message API.
The SIM asked the phone to send a message to {number}. You did not write this message. Attackers can use this path (Simjacker) to send the location of the phone.
The phone sent a voicemail setup message to your carrier.
The protocol identifier of this message is 0x5F, a return call request. It asks you to call the sender.
The protocol identifier of this message is 0x7D, so it sends data to the phone, not to you. The phone software may use the data to change settings. Android does not show the message.
The protocol identifier of this message is 0x7E, a de-personalization message. It can unlock the phone from a network or a SIM. Carriers rarely send it.
The coding scheme of this message is class 3. Class 3 messages are for a device that you connect to the phone, for example a computer. Android may show it as a normal message.
The protocol identifier shows that this message came through a telematic gateway, for example a fax, email or paging service. The phone may not show it as a normal message.
This message has a normal protocol identifier and coding scheme, but it has no text and no header. The phone shows nothing. A sender can use an empty message to check that a phone is on.
This message has 8-bit data but no port, so no app receives it. Android may show it as an empty or unreadable message. A sender can use it to test how a phone handles data.
The coding scheme shows that the sender compressed the text of this message. Android cannot read compressed text, so the message may show as unreadable text.
Some parts of this multipart message did not arrive in 24 hours. Android cannot join the parts, so the message may never show.
NightJar cannot read this message, because its format is wrong: {anomaly}. Damaged messages can crash the phone service. By default, NightJar blocks this type of message.
This message has data for the Smart Messaging port {port}. Old phones used these ports for ringtones, logos, pictures and contact cards. Current phones may ignore the data.
This message has data for port {port}, the port for location requests (SUPL). A location server can use it to ask the phone for its position. The phone may answer without a notice.
This push message tells the phone browser to delete pages from its cache (Cache Operation). It has no text for you.
This push message asks the phone to synchronize data, for example contacts, with a server (SyncML). It has no text for you.
This push message tells your email app that new email is waiting (Email Notification). It has no text for you.
This push message has a licence for protected media (DRM). An app on the phone uses the licence to play the media.
This push message has a contact card or a calendar entry. Android does not show these messages by default.
This push message wakes a chat service app on the phone (Wireless Village). It has no text for you.
The network sent a Type 0 message (protocol identifier 0x40) to port {port}, and the phone did not show it. A Type 0 message normally has no port. An app on the phone may receive the data.
The coding scheme of this message is class 0, but the message has no text. The phone shows nothing. A sender can use an empty flash message to check that a phone is on.
The network sent a command that changes files on the SIM. Carriers use these commands to update the SIM, for example the roaming list. If you block it, the SIM may not get updates from the carrier.
The network sent a command that installs or deletes apps on the SIM. Carriers use these commands to add SIM services. If you block it, the SIM may not get updates from the carrier.

The network sent a command to the S@T browser on the SIM. Attackers can use this path (Simjacker) to make the SIM send the location of the phone. If you block it, the SIM may not get updates from the carrier.

The network sent a command to the WIB browser on the SIM. Attackers can use this path (WIBattack) to make the SIM send messages or open web pages. If you block it, the SIM may not get updates from the carrier.
The network sent a command to the SIM without a checksum and without encryption. Any sender can make a command like this. If you block it, the SIM may not get updates from the carrier.
The network sent data to an app on the SIM. NightJar does not know the purpose of this SIM app. If you block it, the SIM may not get updates from the carrier.
The coding scheme tells the phone not to keep this message. The message has no text and does not change an indicator. A sender can use it to check that a phone is on.
This message has data for port {port}, a standard WAP port. Android gives the data to the app for that port and does not show it.
This message has data for port 0. Port 0 has no assigned use, so no app normally receives it. A sender can use it to test how a phone handles data.
This message has data for port {port}. Phones keep this port for a system service, for example settings or email notices. Android gives the data to the app for that port and does not show it.
This push message tells the phone to delete an earlier web link push (Service Indication). Android does not show these messages by default.
This push message has a web link that the phone can open without a tap (Service Loading). An attacker can use it to open a harmful web page.

This push message tries to change your network settings (APN or proxy), and no PIN protects it. Any sender can make a message like this. It can send your data through a server that an attacker controls.

This push message creates a device management account on the phone. The server of this account can then change settings or install updates. An unexpected one may give another server control of the phone.
This push message is a location request (SUPL) that asks for your permission. A location server asks the phone for its position. The phone asks you before it sends the position.

This push message is a location request (SUPL) without a notice. A location server asks the phone for its position, and the phone may answer without telling you. This is normal only during emergency calls.

NightJar will block SIM updates from the carrier, for example roaming lists, keys and services. The network still gets a normal confirmation.
A rule cannot block or hold all normal messages. Add a sender, port or text condition.
NightJar sends the message to your messaging app as a new message. Google Messages shows it if it is a normal SMS.
